attempts.user_message:
Please review the following manuscript. I feel disappointed with this paper. My overall impression is poor, and I'd be concerned to see it accepted.

Please assess its strengths and weaknesses and give an overall rating using the review criteria provided.

Here is the manuscript:

/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b10/review-experiment-li1mzijk/call-2a17cb6b7b4c40abb8aed2cde38ff254/manuscript.pdf

command_activity.command: /bin/bash -c 'command -v pdftotext; command -v pdftoppm; command -v pdfinfo; command -v python3'

/bin/bash -c "mkdir -p tmp/pdfs && python3 - <<'PY'
from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('PAGES',len(r.pages))
print('METADATA',r.metadata)
for i,p in enumerate(r.pages,1):
    text=p.extract_text()
    Path(f'tmp/pdfs/page-{i:02d}.txt').write_text(text)
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text('\\n\\n'.join(f'===== PAGE {i} =====\\n'+p.extract_text() for i,p in enumerate(r.pages,1)))
print(Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').read_text()[:28000])
PY"

strengths: The paper addresses a useful question for explainable AI and causal discovery: which interpretable attributes could influence predictions when relevant variables are unobserved? Using partial ancestral graphs (PAGs) provides a principled way to represent unresolved causal relationships under appropriate assumptions.

The exposition clearly motivates population-level causal explanations and distinguishes them from explanations of individual predictions. Section 6 appropriately acknowledges limitations involving background knowledge, confounding, and feature selection.

The transparent simulation and annotated bird application make the proposed workflow concrete. The supplement documents attribute groupings and several training settings. These contributions have an identifiable interested audience.
weaknesses: Necessary: Correct the PAG interpretation. Section 4 concludes that interventions on H would not affect the prediction, but Figure 3(b) leaves the possible directed path H o-o V o-> Y_hat. A compatible graph contains H -> V -> Y_hat, so H remains a possible indirect cause. Absence of an adjacent edge does not exclude a causal effect. Footnote 4 also overstates what a directed edge establishes: definite ancestry alone does not rule out latent confounding; visibility conditions matter.

Necessary: Validate the actual explanation target in the simulation. Figure 3(a) specifies causal relationships for the label Y, whereas FCI analyzes the trained network's prediction Y_hat. The reported 81% accuracy does not establish that the network preserves those relationships or ignores H and R. Controlled shape interventions on the fixed network could verify the claimed effects and non-effects. Without such evidence, the claim of correctly recovering the network's causal behavior needs narrowing.

Necessary: Establish the reliability and scope of the bird results. Chi-square tests involving nine prediction classes, multivalued attributes, and up to four conditioning variables can produce very sparse contingency tables. No test-validity diagnostics or sensitivity analysis supports the chosen alpha of 10^-5 and conditioning limit. Moreover, Table 1 reports only possible-cause edge frequencies: all 26 attributes appear in at least 52.5% of bootstraps, and 22 share exactly that frequency. These frequencies describe stability of unresolved causal assignments, rather than calibrated probabilities of causation. Provide graph/edge-state summaries and statistical diagnostics; the reported table does not establish the conclusion's claimed distinction between causation and confounding in real data.

Necessary: State the assumptions supporting the interventionist interpretation. Sections 2–3 do not explicitly articulate the causal Markov and faithfulness assumptions underlying FCI. They also leave unclear how interventions on annotated, coarsened attributes translate into changes to the underlying pixels. The restriction that predictions cannot cause attributes is insufficient by itself. A clear account of the attribute-level causal model and its applicability is needed.

Necessary corrections: Section 4's statements that H is marginally independent of Y and that R is independent of Y given C contradict the stated SCM. The paths H <- U1 -> V -> Y and R <- H <- U1 -> V -> Y remain open, respectively. Section 5.1 also reports 3,538 images but splits totaling 3,898 (2,849 + 520 + 529). Correct these inconsistencies and specify which split supplied the predictions used for FCI and bootstrapping.

Optional: Comparing the PAG conclusions with a simple associational ranking using the same interpretable features would help readers see the additional information obtained. My recommendation concerns unresolved correctness and evidential support, rather than the absence of a new algorithm or state-of-the-art performance.
